position: Correctly orient arms control; Champion the benefits of missile defense
proposal: The Mandate recommends agreeing to arms control only when it advances the interests of the United States and its allies, rejecting disarmament proposals contrary to deterrence, pursuing arms control as a means rather than an end, and preparing to compete if arms control keeps failing. It also recommends rejecting claims that missile defense is destabilizing and committing to keep homeland missile defense out of any arms control talks with Russia and China.

status_summary: New START and its central limits expired on 2026-02-05 without a formal U.S. response to Russia's offer to keep observing them for a year, and the President posted that day that the United States should seek a new, improved and modernized treaty, per the Arms Control Association. On 2026-02-06 Under Secretary of State Thomas DiNanno told the Conference on Disarmament that a bilateral treaty with Russia alone is inappropriate, that a new arrangement must account for all Russian nuclear weapons and China's buildup and meet U.S. verification standards, and that the United States may expand forces if the President directs. On 2026-02-17 Assistant Secretary Christopher Yeaw said the United States had proposed multilateral strategic stability talks; China has said it will not join nuclear disarmament negotiations, and Russia and China criticized the U.S. missile defense plan in a joint statement of 2026-05-20. No official U.S. statement on keeping homeland missile defense out of negotiations was found.

timeline.event: New START expired; the President posted that the United States should seek a new, improved and modernized treaty, and the United States had not formally accepted Russia's proposal to observe the central limits.

Under Secretary of State Thomas DiNanno told the Conference on Disarmament that a new arrangement must account for all Russian nuclear weapons and China's stockpile growth, that a Russia-only treaty is inappropriate, and that U.S. forces could be expanded if the President directs; the remarks were circulated as document CD/2498.
Assistant Secretary of State Christopher Yeaw said at the Hudson Institute that the United States had proposed multilateral strategic stability talks.

title: Orient arms control to U.S. interests and keep homeland missile defense off the table
uncertainties: The President's 2026-02-05 post was not read directly; it and the Yeaw remarks rest on Arms Control Association summaries, an advocacy-leaning research group used here only for those two statements, which the CD/2498 remarks corroborate in substance. The 2026-02-06 remarks were read in the Conference on Disarmament document CD/2498 (issued 2026-02-11), which does not mention missile defense. Per the brief, a posture statement is at most proposed, and absence of an agreement is not an action. The 2026-05-20 Russia and China statement was read through a Reuters item syndicated by TimesLIVE. The Mandate's missile defense exclusion was also listed as not verified in c04-07; no 2025 or 2026 official statement on excluding homeland defense from talks was found. Searches for talks after February 2026 were limited; later developments may have been missed. The agency field names the Department of State as the actor for these statements; the chapter is the Department of Defense chapter.
